To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

no covalent DNA adducts were formed from the nonmutagenic and noncarcinogenic antihistamine methapyrilene or from several other structurally related noncarcinogenic compounds, even when the rats were administered very large doses.

no covalent adduction of methapyrileneto DNA was found in rats treated with this carcinogen, although the adducts from a potent carcinogen, 2-amino 3-methylimidazo[4,5f]quinoline, were readily detected.
methapyrilene (MP) and related noncarcinogenic antihistamines do not react covalently with DNA in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method of analysis for carcinogens and their metabolites in biological samples and with the application of the method to the study of carcinogens and their metabolism.
the development of new analytical methods for the detection of DNA damage, particularly in relation to the carcinogenic action of drugs.
the identification and quantitation of DNA adduct formation in vivo in rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

methapyrilene does not form detectable DNA adducts at doses which produce carcinogenesis in the rat, but the possibility remains that the dose of amine required to induce carcinogenesis is higher than that used in these experiments.

no covalent binding of methapyrilene or any of the other antihistamines tested to DNA of rat liver or other tissues could be detected by the 32P-postlabeling method at a level of sensitivity of 1 in approximately 10(7)-10(8) nucleotides.
methapyrilene does not bind covalently to DNA in the liver of rats treated for 2 or 4 wk at 0.1% of the diet.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the carcinogenicity of methapyrilenes is due to a mechanism which is not mediated by DNA adducts.
the 32P-postlabeling method can detect DNA adducts from mutagenic and carcinogenic chemicals, but not from noncarcinogenic ones.
methapyrilene has not been shown to form DNA adducts at a detectable level in any of the tissues of several species of animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 32P method is a very sensitive method for detecting DNA adducts, but it is not sensitive enough for detecting DNA addducts at the level of one adduct in a million nucleotides.
methapyrilene does not appear to form DNA adducts.
methapyrilene does not bind covalently to DNA in vivo, and that this nonmutagenic compound is not carcinogenic.
